Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance, with the aim of supporting standardized reporting and improving report quality in clinical practice. By facilitating consistent and accurate reporting, such systems have the potential to enhance communication, reduce errors, and improve patient care in radiology.

Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024. The multi-agent AI pipeline consisted of three sequential agents: (1) a structuring agent that first segmented reports into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models; (2) a consistency-checking agent that then detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections or within sections; and (3) a QA agent that subsequently identified gender-anatomy conflicts and undocumented communication of critical findings using rule-based and language model prompts. Each agent operated independently, passing its output to the next agent in sequence; errors or flagged issues were propagated forward, but no automated feedback loops or error correction between agents were implemented in this version. The system’s structuring and QA functions were evaluated together as a unified workflow. For radiologist evaluation, a random subset of 45 reports was selected using stratified random sampling to represent the distribution of body regions and types of flagged issues in the full dataset. Two board-certified radiologists independently reviewed these reports. “Correctly restructured” was defined as accurate anatomical section assignment for the entire report without altering original content; “incorrectly restructured” indicated misassignment or loss of information at the report level; “disagreement” reflected differing reviewer assessments per report. In cases of disagreement, no consensus process was used; each reviewer’s assessment was recorded independently. Inter-rater agreement was calculated using Cohen’s kappa.

Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all 638 reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 of 638 reports (14.1%, 95% CI: 11.5–17.0%), most commonly for section mismatches (80 of 638 reports, 12.5%, 95% CI: 10.1–15.4%). Gender-anatomy conflicts were detected in 5 of 638 reports (0.8%), and undocumented communication of critical findings in 3 of 638 reports (0.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 of 45 reports (69%, 95% CI: 53–82%) were correctly restructured, 2 of 45 reports (4%, 95% CI: 0–13%) were incorrectly restructured, and there was disagreement on 12 of 45 reports (27%, 95% CI: 15–42%). Cohen’s kappa for agreement was 0.62, which is generally interpreted as substantial agreement (with values between 0.61 and 0.80 considered substantial). Both reviewers independently assessed whether any clinically important information was omitted or any fabricated content was introduced, using an open-ended review of each report; both agreed that neither occurred. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" in 24 of 45 reports (53%), "good" in 14 of 45 reports (31%), and "fair" in 7 of 45 reports (16%), corresponding to 38 of 45 reports (84%, 95% CI: 70–93%) rated as "excellent" or "good".

Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow, demonstrating favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. Limitations include the retrospective design, single-institution setting, limited sample size for radiologist evaluation, and potential sources of error such as misclassification of anatomical sections or missed inconsistencies. The system’s generalizability to other institutions, imaging modalities, or report types remains to be established. Future work will focus on expanding the system to additional report types, incorporating automated feedback mechanisms between agents, and further improving error detection. The study was conducted with institutional review board approval and in compliance with data privacy regulations; all data were anonymized and stored on secure, access-controlled servers. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.

REVIEW:
